strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: reducing quadratic attention cost in video diffusion transformers without costly full pretraining, via a data-free post-training approach.

The selective transfer formulation (treating per-layer attention type as a learnable, differentiable binary choice with STE and a target-count constraint) is a reasonably novel and practical solution to the layer-selection problem, and the paper provides clear empirical motivation (Fig. 2/3) for why naive/manual/heuristic layer choices are suboptimal.

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is a sensible adaptation of distribution-matching distillation to the post-training linearization setting; using the model itself to estimate its own score avoids training an auxiliary large model, yielding a claimed 4.4x training-time reduction versus DMD-style objectives, which is empirically validated (Table 4, Fig. 8).

Reasonably thorough ablations: target ratio, selective transfer vs manual/heuristic baselines, regularization term Lreg, and objective comparisons (Lmse, LDMD, ADM with/without extra score network) are all provided with quantitative VBench numbers.

Results are evaluated on both VBench and the more challenging VBench-2.0, and the method is shown to be combinable with few-step distillation (DMD2) for a large end-to-end 15.92x speedup with only minor quality loss, plus qualitative visualizations are provided.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single, relatively small model (Wan 1.3B) at a fixed low resolution (832x480) and fixed video length (5s/16fps); it is unclear whether the approach scales to larger, more competitive video DMs (e.g., 14B) or higher resolutions/longer sequences, which is where quadratic attention costs matter most and where the paper's motivation is strongest.

The achieved end-to-end speedups (1.25-2.00x without the distillation) are modest, and the paper explicitly notes no specialized kernel is used, making it hard to judge the real deployable benefit versus sparse-attention baselines that also lack full optimization; the comparison of 'fair' baseline implementations (excluding specialized kernels/RMSNorm) could bias the speedup comparison in the method's favor.

No direct empirical comparison to the mentioned concurrent work SLA (intra-layer mixed attention) or to prior linear-attention pretraining methods (SANA-Video, LinGen, TTT) is provided, even though these are the most relevant points of comparison for judging how much of the quadratic-to-linear performance gap is closed; comparisons are restricted to sparsification baselines, which address a different efficiency mechanism.

The quality differences reported in the main table (e.g., 66.07 vs 66.25 Imaging Quality, differences often <1 point) are very small and no statistical significance or human study is provided, making it difficult to assess whether the method is truly 'lossless' or just within measurement noise of VBench metrics.

The target replacement ratio is fixed per experiment and appears to require retuning/re-training per desired speedup level (Table 2, Fig. 6 sweep over target=10..20), without a clear automatic mechanism to choose target for a new model or deployment budget, partially undercutting the 'automatic' framing of selective transfer.

The derivation and practical use of ADM is specific to rectified-flow/velocity-parameterized models with a particular score estimation trick (Eq. 13); applicability to standard epsilon-prediction diffusion models or other schedules is not discussed or validated.

Method description leaves some reproducibility gaps: e.g., exact schedule for annealing alpha in Lreg, sensitivity to initialization of r, and the procedure used to build the 'Heuristic' grid-search baseline are deferred to the appendix (not included here), which limits ability to fully verify claims from the main text alone.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reducing quadratic self-attention cost in video diffusion transformers without costly full pretraining, which is highly relevant given the deployment bottleneck of long-sequence video DMs.

The selective transfer formulation (learnable binary classification score with straight-through estimator, constraint and regularization losses) is a principled and automatic alternative to manual/heuristic layer selection, and the ablation (Table 3) convincingly shows it outperforms both manual and heuristic layer choices.

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is a well-motivated technical contribution: it avoids the need to train an auxiliary score-estimation network (unlike DMD-style objectives) by reusing the current multi-step model to estimate its own score, yielding a claimed ~4.4x training-time reduction while improving quality over naive MSE and standard distribution matching losses (Table 4, Fig. 6).

Experiments span two model scales (Wan 1.3B and Wan 14B) and two benchmarks (VBench and the more challenging VBench-2.0), plus latency measurements against multiple recent sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, XAttention, DFA), lending reasonably broad empirical support.

The paper demonstrates a practical two-stage pipeline combining linearization with few-step distillation (DMD2), achieving large additional speedups (15.9-20.9x) with modest quality degradation, and explicitly shows that naively combining the two in one stage collapses performance (Appendix F), which is a useful empirical finding.
Derivations (e.g., Eq. 13) and design choices (regularization scheduling, α ablation) are documented with reasonable transparency in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of specific components.
weaknesses: The reported speedup gains over the strongest sparse-attention baseline are relatively modest (1.43x vs. SVG's 1.31x on 1.3B, 1.71x vs. SVG's 1.61x on 14B), and the authors do not employ a specialized attention kernel for their own method, making the true achievable speedup and a fair head-to-head efficiency comparison uncertain until such an implementation exists.

No baseline is provided comparing against directly linearizing all layers with the same data-free/ADM training budget, which would more sharply demonstrate the necessity of selective transfer versus simply reducing target further; the paper only ablates target values on top of the already-selective method.

All experiments are conducted on a single model family (Wan 1.3B/14B); generalization of the selective transfer + ADM framework to other DiT-based video DMs (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo) with different architectures/attention configurations is not empirically verified, limiting evidence of broader applicability.

Comparison to the concurrent and closely related SLA method is omitted entirely (even without latency, a quality-only comparison would be informative) on the grounds of kernel-specific hardware requirements, leaving readers unable to judge relative effectiveness of the core algorithmic contributions.

The target number of linearized layers is fixed prior to training and requires separate training runs per target; the paper does not discuss the additional training cost incurred by the selective transfer stage itself relative to a fixed-layer ADM-only baseline, obscuring the total post-training overhead.

Evaluation relies solely on automated VBench/VBench-2.0 metrics; no human preference study or finer-grained analysis of failure modes (e.g., specific content types where linear attention underperforms) is provided, which would strengthen claims of "preserving performance."

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: reducing quadratic attention cost in video DMs via data-free post-training, avoiding costly full pretraining required by prior linear-attention approaches.

The selective transfer method is well-motivated by an empirical observation (Fig. 2/3) that layer replaceability varies significantly, and the binary-classification framing with STE + regularization is a sensible, differentiable solution validated against manual and heuristic baselines (Tab. 3).

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is a clear technical contribution: it avoids the need for an auxiliary score-estimation model (unlike DMD-style objectives), yielding ~4.4x training-time reduction while improving quality (Tab. 4, Fig. 6), and the derivation (Eq. 13) is provided in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation across two model scales (1.3B and 14B), two benchmarks (VBench and the more challenging VBench-2.0), multiple sparse-attention baselines, and both quantitative and qualitative results, plus thorough ablations of nearly every design choice (target, λ, α, selective transfer, ADM).

Practical impact is demonstrated by combining with few-step distillation (DMD2) for large additional speedups (15.9-20.9x) with modest quality loss, and the paper appropriately notes complementary future directions (sparse attention integration, custom kernels).

Reasonably honest positioning relative to concurrent work (SLA) and clear discussion of why naive alternatives (Lmse, standard distribution matching) fail in this setting, backed by ablation evidence.
weaknesses: The speedup numbers (1.43-1.71x) are measured without any specialized kernel implementation for the mixed dense linear/quadratic attention, which the authors acknowledge; this makes it hard to assess the real-world deployment benefit versus kernel-optimized baselines like SVG/SVG2, and the comparison to sparse-attention methods may not be fully apples-to-apples in terms of engineering effort.

The core techniques (binary layer selection via learnable scores + STE, distribution matching aligned with score-based generative modeling ideas) are adaptations of established techniques from quantization/NAS and diffusion distillation literature rather than fundamentally new mechanisms; novelty is more in the specific combination and application to video DM linearization.

Evaluation is limited to a single base model family (Wan 1.3B/14B); generalization to other architectures (CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, etc.) is not demonstrated, so it's unclear how sensitive the method is to architecture-specific properties.

The layer-selection experiments in Fig. 2 that motivate the method are based on only a small set of configurations (10-layer blocks), and the underlying reasons for why certain layers (e.g., the first layer) are catastrophic are only briefly hypothesized, without deeper mechanistic analysis.

Some quantitative gains over the strongest sparse-attention baseline (SVG2) on VBench metrics are marginal (often <1 point), and the paper's own dense FlashAttention2 baseline is sometimes matched or only slightly exceeded, so the claimed 'lossless acceleration' should be interpreted cautiously given VBench metric sensitivity/noise across only 3-5 samples per prompt.

The ADM derivation relies on treating the partially-linearized model as a rectified-flow model throughout training and using the model's own predictions to estimate its score function, which is a reasonable approximation but its theoretical justification (accuracy of self-estimated score under a shifting, non-final linear-attention model) is not rigorously established beyond empirical validation.
